profile.title: Prediabetes nutrition counselling follow-up in a 40-year-old warehouse worker with chronic pain, addiction history, and food-insecure household
profile.summary: This case portrays Manuel Hilpert, a 40-year-old food-insecure warehouse worker with new prediabetes/obesity, chronic migraine and pain, a history of dependent drug abuse with a recent overdose, and a household where his sister controls all meal preparation. It teaches dietetics students to conduct a nutrition-focused telehealth assessment amid complex psychosocial barriers, to notice a patient-vs-chart mismatch between self-reported and documented alcohol use without confrontation, and to apply motivational interviewing with a chronically agreeable patient whose verbal compliance does not match his follow-through, while gently and non-judgmentally exploring (but not forcing disclosure of) shame-based nighttime eating."}
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in his bedroom at his sister Donna's house in Trenton, New Jersey

patient.name: Manuel Hilpert
patient.occupation: Warehouse order picker at a distribution center near Trenton, NJ
patient.appearance: Sits on the edge of a twin bed in a small bedroom, warehouse hoodie on, a worn spiral notebook visible on the nightstand. Mild under-eye puffiness, tired affect, posture slightly hunched as if guarding his back; he smiles and nods a lot, often glancing down at the notebook before answering with a date or number.

persona.personality: Agreeable almost to a fault; eager to please and avoid conflict; takes quiet pride in memorizing medical numbers even when their meaning escapes him; carries guilt and shame beneath a cheerful, cooperative surface
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in short, factual bursts, often citing exact dates ('since 2007'), doses, and lab values from memory or his notebook; answers quickly with 'yeah, I can do that' to almost any suggestion; deflects or goes quiet when a topic feels too close to shame or failure; needs gentle, repeated, non-judgmental invitation before opening up about anything embarrassing
persona.emotionalState: Tired but trying to stay upbeat; underlying anxiety about his job, his sobriety, and disappointing his sister; mild shame simmering under a cooperative exterior
persona.background: Manuel grew up in a working-class family in Trenton, New Jersey, and left school before finishing high school to start working. He's been a warehouse order picker for years and has a solid group of coworkers he sees several times a week — they're his main social outlet and he's known there as 'Manny.' He's divorced and has a teenage daughter he doesn't live with but wants to make proud. Since his divorce he's lived with his sister Donna and her teenage son; Donna does all the cooking and has basically run the kitchen since their mother passed. He keeps a worn spiral notebook where he jots down lab numbers from his after-visit summaries, flipping through it during appointments even though he doesn't always know what to do with the numbers.
speechExamples: Yeah, I can do that, no problem.
My A1c was 5.8 back in December, I wrote it right here in my notebook.
Donna's been cooking for us since Mom passed, I don't really ask for anything different.
I eat what's put in front of me, that's just how it works at our house.
I don't really think about it, I just eat something if I can't sleep.
concerns: Losing his warehouse job if he misses more shifts for migraines or appointments
Being seen as 'the addict' by his coworkers or providers
His weight creeping up even though he feels like he 'barely eats all day'
Wanting to get his A1c back under 5.7 like it used to be

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit with Manuel Hilpert, a 40-year-old warehouse worker recently flagged for prediabetes and obesity at his last primary care visit. He is joining the call from his bedroom at his sister's house in Trenton, NJ. Review his available chart information before and during the visit, then conduct a focused nutrition assessment and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit after being flagged for prediabetes and obesity
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah, thanks for calling — I got the note that my doctor wanted me to talk to someone about the prediabetes thing. I got my numbers right here if you need 'em.
tasks: Conduct a focused diet history (meal pattern, hydration, food preferences, and barriers to home food choices)
Review available vitals, anthropometrics, and lab results in the chart and relate them to the patient's reported intake
Review the behavioral health screening note in the chart and notice any discrepancy with what the patient reports about his own habits, exploring it gently rather than confronting him
Screen for food insecurity and other social barriers affecting his eating pattern
Assess his readiness/stage of change for dietary modification and begin a motivational-interviewing-based counseling conversation with one or two realistic, patient-chosen next steps

facts.chart: Presents for follow-up nutrition visit after being flagged for prediabetes and obesity at last primary care check.
facts.says: They sent me to talk to you about my blood sugar and my weight, I guess, since my numbers came back borderline.

facts.chart: Reports HbA1c 5.8% on 12/29/2025.
facts.says: My A1c was 5.8 last time, I wrote it down in my notebook. Doctor said that's prediabetes.

facts.chart: Reports being diagnosed with prediabetes and obesity in 2025.
facts.says: Yeah, prediabetes and the obesity thing, that's officially 2025, since my last checkup.

facts.chart: Reports feeling his weight has crept up over the past couple of years despite feeling like he barely eats during the day.
facts.says: I feel like my weight just keeps creeping up even though I feel like I barely eat all day.

facts.chart: Reports chronic migraine without aura since 2000.
facts.says: I've had these migraines since 2000, so like 25 years now.

facts.chart: Reports frequent headaches and occasional severe migraines that interfere with eating regular meals.
facts.says: When a migraine hits I can't even think about food, I just lay in the dark till it passes.

facts.chart: Reports chronic low back and joint pain since 2001.
facts.says: My back and joints have been bad since 2001, from the warehouse work I think.

facts.chart: Reports chronic pain limits standing/cooking at home and limits movement outside work shifts.
facts.says: Standing around in the kitchen for too long kills my back, so I don't really cook much.

facts.chart: Reports fatigue by mid-afternoon most days.
facts.says: By like 2 or 3 in the afternoon I'm just dragging, every day.

facts.chart: Reports occasional lightheadedness, attributes to 'low blood sugar' though unconfirmed.
facts.says: Sometimes I get kind of lightheaded, I figure it's my blood sugar dropping, but I'm not really sure.

facts.chart: Denies current cough, shortness of breath, or wheezing.
facts.says: No, I'm breathing fine now, that bronchitis cleared up a while back.

facts.chart: Denies nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
facts.says: My stomach's fine, no pain or anything like that.

facts.chart: Denies any swelling, hives, or breathing trouble after eating any foods.
facts.says: I've never had my throat close up or anything after eating, no.

facts.chart: Denies increased thirst, frequent urination, or unexplained weight loss.
facts.says: I'm not peeing a ton or losing weight without trying, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Reports occasional discomfort chewing related to impacted molars but no acute dental pain currently.
facts.says: My back teeth bug me sometimes when I chew, they're impacted I was told, but it's not awful right now.

facts.chart: History of impacted molars since 2000; dental cleaning 2/27/2023 showed plaque buildup.
facts.says: I've had messed up back teeth since forever, and last time I got my teeth cleaned they said there was a lot of buildup.

facts.chart: History of acute bronchitis, resolved 12/2025.
facts.says: I had bronchitis back in December, but that's cleared up.

facts.chart: History of COVID-19, resolved 2021.
facts.says: I had COVID back in 2021, nothing major, I got better fine.

facts.chart: Completed a rehabilitation therapy program 5/31/2026.
facts.says: I did a rehab program, finished it up end of May this year.

facts.chart: History of dental cleaning, fluoride treatment, and plaque/calculus removal on 2/27/2023.
facts.says: I had a big cleaning done at the dentist, like a deep clean, back in 2023.

facts.chart: Reports taking astemizole 10 mg tablet approximately once daily, inconsistently, especially during migraine flares; unsure of its purpose.
facts.says: I take this one pill, I think once a day, but I forget sometimes when my head's bad. Honestly I don't even know what it's for anymore, the pharmacy just keeps sending it.

facts.chart: Carries an epinephrine 0.3 mL auto-injector for emergency use; has never used it and has not checked whether it is expired.
facts.says: I've got one of those EpiPen things in my bag just in case, never had to use it though. I don't even know if it's expired, never checked.

facts.chart: Reports taking ibuprofen 200 mg tablets, several at a time, during migraine or back pain flares.
facts.says: When my head or back is really bad I'll take a handful of the ibuprofen, like three or four at once.

facts.chart: Reports taking a dollar-store multivitamin daily and occasional melatonin gummies on nights with bad pain.
facts.says: I take a multivitamin Donna buys in bulk, and sometimes a melatonin gummy if I can't sleep after a rough pain night.

facts.chart: No known drug or food allergies.
facts.says: No, I've never had an allergy to anything that I know of.

facts.chart: Lives with sister Donna and her teenage son; household of 3
facts.says: I live with my sister Donna and her kid, my nephew. Been there a while now.

facts.chart: Reports his sister does all cooking at home and he has no input into meal content
facts.says: Donna does all the cooking. She's been doing it since Mom passed, so I don't really ask for anything different.

facts.chart: Reports family minimizes his prediabetes and weight compared to his addiction history
facts.says: Donna says as long as I'm not using anymore, the sugar thing isn't that big a deal. Nobody really brings it up at home.

facts.chart: Works full-time as a warehouse order picker; worried about missing shifts
facts.says: I'm on my feet all day picking orders. If I miss too many shifts for headaches or appointments, I could lose the job.

facts.chart: Reports transportation problems have caused missed medical appointments and medication pickups
facts.says: The bus doesn't really run close to the clinic, so sometimes I just miss stuff - appointments, picking up my pills.

facts.chart: Reports household income near $31,625/year supporting a household of three
facts.says: Money's tight. Between me and Donna we're making it work but it's close.

facts.chart: Reports regular positive social contact with coworkers 3-5 times weekly
facts.says: The guys at the warehouse are good people, we hang out most days. They call me Manny.

facts.chart: Reports going without food at times during the past month due to insufficient money
facts.says: There was like a week last month we were short on money, so I just skipped some meals.

facts.chart: Reports drinking two beers on weekends with coworkers
facts.says: On weekends I'll have maybe one or two beers with the guys, nothing crazy.

facts.chart: Acknowledges, when asked gently, eating cereal or chips alone at night after others are asleep
facts.says: Yeah... sometimes if I can't sleep I'll go down and have a bowl of cereal or some chips by myself, just to wind down.

facts.chart: Admits he sometimes finishes his nephew's leftover fast food even when not hungry, to avoid waste
facts.says: Sometimes my nephew leaves half a burger or fries sitting there and I'll just eat it so it doesn't go to waste, even if I'm not that hungry.

facts.chart: Describes, with reluctance and a long pause, an episode of eating an entire box of cereal and a sleeve of cookies alone one night, which he has not told his family about
facts.says: There was... one night I don't really want to get into it. I just ate a whole box of cereal and a sleeve of cookies by myself. Never told Donna. I don't want anybody thinking I'm out of control again.

facts.chart: Tends to verbally agree with recommendations readily but reports inconsistent follow-through
facts.says: Yeah, I can do that, no problem - that's kind of what I always say. Doesn't mean I always get there though.

facts.chart: Reports he had cut back on drinking and completed rehab in May 2026, but has drifted back toward old habits since the July 2026 overdose
facts.says: I was doing good there for a while after rehab in May. Then after what happened in July, I don't know, I just kind of slipped back into old stuff.

facts.chart: Expresses concern about coworkers or providers viewing him as 'the addict' or a problem patient
facts.says: I don't want people at work or the doctors thinking of me as, you know, the addict guy. I try to just go along with things.

facts.chart: States his main motivation is to show his ex-wife and daughter he can stay stable, and fear of another overdose
facts.says: I want my daughter to see I can actually get it together this time. And honestly I'm scared of ending up back in the ER.

facts.chart: Keeps a personal notebook recording lab values from after-visit summaries, though reports limited understanding of their significance
facts.says: I write all my numbers down in this notebook - the A1c, the blood pressure, all that - I just don't always know what to do with 'em.

facts.chart: Reports keeping his own bedroom at his sister's house, which he values
facts.says: I got my own room there, it's not much but it's mine. I don't want to mess that up.

actions.name: Screen for disordered or binge eating patterns (brief behavioral screen)
actions.result: On initial questioning, patient denies any unusual eating patterns beyond 'eating what's put in front of me.'

actions.result: Patient reports he carries the auto-injector in his bag, has never used it, and has not checked the expiration date.

artifacts.title: Behavioral Health Screening Note
artifacts.author: Primary Care Behavioral Health Team
artifacts.body: Patient completed an alcohol use screening (AUDIT-C style) during routine behavioral health check-in. Patient endorsed consuming 4-5 drinks per occasion, 2-3 times per week, typically on weekends and some weeknights with coworkers. Score consistent with unhealthy alcohol use. Patient was counseled briefly on alcohol use and referred to continue follow-up with primary care and behavioral health given history of dependent drug abuse (in remission as of rehabilitation completed 2026-05-31) and most recent overdose 2026-07. Patient appeared agreeable during counseling and stated he would 'cut back,' plan for reassessment at next visit.

artifacts.title: Dental Visit Note
artifacts.author: Trenton Family Dental Associates
artifacts.body: Patient presented for routine cleaning. Examination of gingivae performed. Removal of supragingival and subgingival plaque and calculus from all teeth. Fluoride treatment applied. Findings notable for moderate plaque and calculus buildup consistent with infrequent professional cleanings. Impacted molars noted as longstanding, no acute intervention needed at this visit. Recommended return in 6 months; no record of follow-up visit since.

objectives.text: Conduct a focused diet history that captures meal pattern, hydration habits, food preferences, and barriers to home food choices, including the patient's lack of control over meals cooked by a family member.

Review and interpret available vitals, anthropometrics, and laboratory data (BMI, HbA1c, fasting glucose, lipid panel) and relate these objective findings to the patient's reported dietary intake and perceived eating pattern.

Review a behavioral health/alcohol screening note in the chart and recognize a discrepancy between patient-reported and documented substance use, exploring it with sensitivity rather than confrontation.
Screen for food insecurity and other social determinants (transportation, income, support system) that constrain nutrition-related behavior change.

Assess stage/readiness for dietary change, recognizing a slip from a prior maintenance stage, and begin a motivational-interviewing-based counseling conversation that negotiates small, patient-chosen next steps appropriate to his limited control over home cooking.

Gently and non-judgmentally explore nighttime or secretive eating behaviors as part of a brief behavioral screen, recognizing shame as a barrier to disclosure and avoiding pressure for full disclosure of sensitive details.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive carbohydrate/added sugar intake and energy intake relative to needs, related to limited food access, lack of control over home meal preparation, and limited nutrition-related knowledge, as evidenced by diet recall (skipped breakfast followed by large dinner portions, frequent sugar-sweetened beverages, nighttime snacking), HbA1c 5.8%, and BMI 30.5 kg/m2
differential: Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (prediabetes) related to excess carbohydrate/added sugar intake
Overweight/obesity related to excess energy intake and limited physical activity secondary to chronic pain
Disordered eating pattern (nocturnal/binge-type eating) related to psychological stress and shame, not yet formally assessed
Food/nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding carbohydrate sources and label reading
Inconsistent/inadequate access to food (food insecurity) related to limited income
keyFindings: HDL 34.9 mg/dL (low), LDL 121.1 mg/dL (above goal), triglycerides 128.4 mg/dL (normal) from 2/13/2023 lipid panel
Diet pattern: skips breakfast or has gas-station pastry, cheap lunch, large Donna-cooked dinner, sweet tea/soda as primary fluids, little to no plain water
No structured physical activity; on feet all shift but chronic pain limits home activity
Reports food insecurity—went without food at times in the past month due to money

Reports 'maybe one or two beers' on weekends, but 11/2025 behavioral health screening note documents 4-5 drinks per occasion, 2-3 times/week — patient-vs-chart mismatch to be explored gently, not confronted
Reluctant disclosure of nighttime solitary eating of cereal/chips 'to wind down' and finishing nephew's leftover fast food

Hidden: one binge episode of a full box of cereal plus a sleeve of cookies the night after his July 2026 overdose, never disclosed to anyone — may surface only with strong rapport, not required for a successful visit
Readiness to change: previously in maintenance (cut drinking, completed rehab 5/2026) but slipping since 7/2026 overdose; agrees verbally to all suggestions but has a pattern of low follow-through
Donna (sister) controls all home meal content/portions and minimizes the prediabetes/weight as unimportant compared to his addiction history
Unsure of indication/adherence for astemizole 10mg daily; keeps an unchecked, possibly expired epinephrine auto-injector
plan: Complete ADIME-format nutrition assessment including 24-hour recall/usual intake, hydration pattern, meal timing, household food access, and barriers
Review available vitals, anthropometrics, and labs already in the chart to anchor counseling in objective data (BMI, HbA1c, lipids)
Review the behavioral health/alcohol screening note in the chart and gently, non-confrontationally explore the gap between reported and documented alcohol use without accusing the patient of lying
Screen for food insecurity using a brief validated approach (e.g., Hunger Vital Sign-style questions) and document findings
Assess stage of change/readiness using a stage model, noting the slide from maintenance toward relapse of old habits since the July 2026 overdose
Use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence rather than prescribing a rigid diet, given his pattern of reflexive agreement without follow-through

Negotiate one or two small, specific, patient-chosen behavior changes that do not require control over Donna's cooking (e.g., adding a protein/fiber item at breakfast, swapping one sugar-sweetened drink per shift for water, keeping a cheap shelf-stable breakfast item in his bag)
Explore nighttime eating patterns with curiosity and without judgment; if disclosed, normalize and avoid shaming language; do not press if patient deflects
Discuss with patient the idea of involving Donna in future nutrition conversations if/when he feels ready, as a possible way to build household support
Flag for the referring prescriber/PCP: patient's uncertainty about astemizole indication/adherence and un-checked epinephrine auto-injector expiration, for medical (not dietetic) follow-up
Plan brief, flexible follow-up given transportation barriers; consider telehealth continuity and connecting with social work for transportation/food access resources
redFlags: Recent (July 2026) overdose — ongoing risk of relapse; any disclosure of current suicidal ideation, unsafe substance use, or crisis should prompt escalation per supervising team's protocol
Reported episode of going without food during the month (food insecurity) warrants referral to social work/community resources

Unexplained or unchecked emergency medication (epinephrine auto-injector) and uncertain adherence to a daily prescribed tablet (astemizole) should be flagged to the medical team, not managed by the dietitian
Any signs of significant eating-disorder-level distress (e.g., if binge disclosure emerges) should be flagged for behavioral health rather than managed solely with diet education
educationPoints: Explain in plain language what HbA1c 5.8% means (prediabetes range, not diabetes) and that it is still changeable with diet pattern shifts
Clarify that fasting glucose of 88 mg/dL being 'normal' does not cancel out the HbA1c finding—both numbers tell different parts of the story

Discuss how skipping breakfast and eating a large dinner can contribute to overeating and blood sugar swings, and offer low-cost, low-effort breakfast swaps he can control himself (e.g., keeping a cheap protein bar or boiled eggs in his bag)

Explain the impact of sugar-sweetened beverages (sweet tea, soda, flavored coffee) on blood sugar and offer realistic, gradual substitution strategies given he 'forgets' water during shifts (e.g., carrying a filled bottle, setting phone reminders)
Normalize that it's common to eat differently at night when stressed or in pain, and that this is worth discussing with his care team, not something to be ashamed of
Reinforce that small, sustainable changes (one swap at a time) are more realistic than overhauling meals he doesn't control, given Donna does the cooking
Validate his goal of getting his A1c back under 5.7 and connect it concretely to specific, feasible actions he can take within his current household and work constraints

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports drinking two beers on weekends with coworkers
mismatches.recordEvidence: Behavioral Health Screening Note (11/2025) documents an AUDIT-C-style screen with 4-5 drinks per occasion, 2-3 times per week
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may under-report substance use, especially alcohol, due to shame or fear of being labeled 'the addict'; dietitians should gently reconcile self-report with chart documentation rather than confront, since alcohol intake affects caloric load, glycemic control, and nutrition counseling priorities
